passages.t: Who has raised up one from the east?
passages.happening:
God calls the nations to court. ‘Be silent before Me, O islands, and let the peoples renew their strength’ (verse 1). Let them come forward and testify.

‘Who has aroused one from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness?’ (verse 2). He hands nations over to him and brings down kings; he pursues them and passes on safely, hardly touching the path (verses 2-3). Who has done this? The LORD, the first and the last: ‘I am He’ (verse 4).

The islands see it and are afraid; the ends of the earth tremble (verse 5). Each one tells his neighbor, Be strong (verse 6). The craftsman encourages the goldsmith; the one with the hammer cheers on the one at the anvil, and says of the soldering that it is good, and nails the idol down so it will not fall over (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 40 told the exiles that God was coming and that no one could be compared with him. Chapter 41 puts that claim to a public test. A world power is rising in the east, and the nations are frightened. Who is behind it?

The conqueror is not yet named. Chapters 44 and 45 will name him: Cyrus of Persia, who united the Medes and Persians in the 550s BC, conquered Lydia in Asia Minor in the 540s, and took Babylon in 539.

The trial scenes draw on the old practice of settling disputes at the city gate, where both sides presented their case and called witnesses. Here God is both a party and the judge.

Verses 6 and 7 are satire. The frightened craftsmen encourage one another, check the soldering, and nail the statue down so it will not topple. The nations' response to a terrifying new power is to make more gods, and make sure they do not fall over.
passages.later: The risen Christ uses God's title from verse 4: ‘Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last’ (Revelation 1:17).
passages.asks: When the nations were afraid, they made more idols and nailed them down. Ask what you reach for when you are frightened by change. And ask whether you believe that the LORD is first and last, before and after the powers that frighten you.

passages.t: Do not fear, O worm of Jacob
passages.happening:
‘But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend’ (verse 8). God brought them from the ends of the earth and chose them, and has not rejected them (verse 9).

‘Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My right hand of righteousness’ (verse 10). All who rage against them will be put to shame (verses 11-12). ‘For I am the LORD your God, who takes hold of your right hand’ (verse 13).

‘Do not fear, O worm of Jacob, O few men of Israel. I will help you’ (verse 14). ‘Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 14). God will make them a new threshing sledge with sharp teeth that will thresh the mountains (verse 15).

‘The poor and needy seek water, but there is none; their tongues are parched with thirst. I, the LORD, will answer them’ (verse 17). He will open rivers on bare heights and turn the desert into pools (verse 18). He will plant cedars, acacias, myrtles and olives in the wilderness (verse 19), so that all may see that the hand of the LORD has done it (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Here the word servant appears for the first time in these chapters, and it is used for the whole people of Israel. It will be a key word in chapters 41 to 53, and readers should watch how its meaning grows.

God calls Abraham his friend, and Israel the descendants of that friend. The exiles, few and scattered, felt like worms in the dust. God does not deny it. He calls them worm, and then says he will help them.

A threshing sledge was a heavy board set with sharp stones or iron teeth underneath, dragged over grain to break the husks. The weak worm of Jacob becomes a tool that levels mountains.

The road home from Babylon ran through desert. The promise of rivers and trees in the wilderness is a picture of God providing for his people on the way, as he did in the first exodus.
passages.later: James calls Abraham ‘a friend of God’ (James 2:23), as Jehoshaphat had prayed to the God who gave the land ‘to the descendants of Abraham Your friend’ (2 Chronicles 20:7).
passages.asks: God called his people worm and then promised to hold their right hand. Ask whether you feel small and few today. And ask what it would mean to let God take hold of your hand and say, do not fear.

passages.happening:
‘Present your case,’ says the LORD (verse 21). Let the idols tell what will happen, or explain the former things so that people can know the outcome (verse 22). ‘Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods’ (verse 23). Do something, good or bad.

‘Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value’ (verse 24).

God has raised up one from the north, one from the east who calls on his name, who will tread on rulers like a potter treading clay (verse 25). Who announced this from the beginning? No one (verse 26). God was the first to tell Zion, and he sent Jerusalem a herald of good news (verse 27). When he looks among the idols, there is no counselor and no answer (verse 28). ‘See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind’ (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The test proposed is prediction. Gods who cannot say what will happen, or explain what has happened, are not gods at all. In Babylon, divination was a serious and learned business, with experts reading omens in the livers of sacrificed animals and in the movements of the stars. The chapter's challenge strikes at that whole system.

Ancient worshipers did not believe a statue was simply the god. They held that the god was present in the image once it had been ritually consecrated. Many scholars think Isaiah knew this and was attacking the claim at its root: if the gods are real, let them act and speak in history. The silence of the idols is the argument.

The one from the north and the east is usually taken as Cyrus again, whose empire lay to the east of Babylon and whose conquests had already reached Lydia in Asia Minor.
passages.later: God makes the same challenge later: ‘I declare the end from the beginning, and ancient times from what is still to come’ (Isaiah 46:10). A psalm makes the same charge against idols: ‘They have mouths, but cannot speak’ (Psalm 115:5).
passages.hard:
The chapter mocks the idols as nothing. Is that fair to the religions of Israel's neighbors?

Ancient worshipers in Babylon held that the deity was present in the image after it had been consecrated, much as a king was present through his representatives. So a reader may wonder whether Isaiah's satire of carpenters and goldsmiths misses the point. Many scholars answer that Isaiah knew exactly what worshipers believed and attacked the claim at its root: if the gods are real, let them act and speak. Others note that the chapter's main argument is not the making of idols but their silence, and that this argument is aimed at claims, not at people.

The prophet's harshest words elsewhere are spoken to Israel's own leaders, and the invitation later in these chapters to all the ends of the earth (45:22) shows that the goal is not scorn but conversion. Nothing here gives anyone leave to treat people of other faiths with contempt.
passages.asks: God says the idols cannot tell the future or do anything at all. Ask what you consult about the future in place of God. And ask whether your faith rests on a God who has spoken and acted in history, or on one you have to prop up.
